content.overview: A complex case should begin as an evidence inventory, not a diagnosis. Direct observations, measurements, records, test results, images, environmental context and missing information must be separated so weak evidence does not acquire false authority through repetition.

vocabulary.definition: A finding actually seen or measured, recorded without assigning a causal interpretation.
A verified condition such as crop stage, irrigation history, movement record or environmental measurement relevant to interpretation.
An unverified proposition used provisionally and clearly labeled as such.

sections.title: Normalize the case file
sections.body: Reconcile plant/lot IDs, timestamps, room/location, crop stage, sample IDs, units and source of each observation before reasoning from the evidence.

sections.title: Grade evidence by what it can support
sections.body: A photo can support a visible morphology claim; a calibrated measurement can support a value; a laboratory result can support only the identified sample and method. Do not let one evidence type answer questions it was not designed to answer.

sections.title: Record missing and conflicting information
sections.body: Missing denominators, uncertain sample identity, changed monitoring methods and contradictory records should be explicit because they change the confidence of later conclusions.

workedExamples: An image showing leaf chlorosis, an EC measurement from a different irrigation zone and a verbal claim of 'root rot' belong in three different evidence categories and should not be merged into one confirmed diagnosis.
commonMistakes: Starting with the suspected diagnosis and sorting evidence to fit it.
Treating copied notes as independent evidence.
content.practicalApplication: Convert a mixed case packet into a table with evidence ID, source, time, identity, observation, reliability limits, interpretation and missing follow-up.
content.summary: Case quality depends on evidence discipline before diagnosis begins.
